newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Seoul risks sea of inflation as it lets won sink.
newsitem.headline: Seoul risks sea of inflation as it lets won sink.

text.p: South Korean financial authorities, under pressure to cut a rising trade deficit, are allowing the won to sink to record lows but this risks fuelling inflation, economists and dealers said on Tuesday.
"They've decided to leave the won alone because of a huge trade deficit," said Lee Chang-sun, a researcher at LG Economic Research Institute.

Shin Hoo-shik at the Daewoo Economic Research Institute said policymakers feel they have been driven into a corner by the record high trade deficit, which some economists say could reach $20 billion this year.
"They are more comfortable handling inflation," Shin said.
The won remained weak on Tuesday after dropping to an all-time low against the dollar the previous day.
The currency plunged to a low of 829.90 before the central bank came to the rescue and ended little changed.
But Lee Dong-lag, a trader at Korea First Bank, said he did not believe the won had hit bottom and could fall again on Wednesday on renewed dollar buying.
"Banks will buy dollars to cover both expected import deals towards the week's end and short dollar positions," he said.
Dealers said the central bank intervened repeatedly on Monday to slow the won's fall, and stepped in twice again on Tuesday. The bank routinely denies intervention.
Some economists said the government's focus was now on boosting the nation's price competitiveness.
A weak won makes exports cheaper, but also risks inflation by driving up the cost of imports. South Korea relies heavily on imported raw materials and capital equipment.
"The government has been put a difficult spot with local exporters pushing for the won's depreciation," said Lee.

South Korea's trade deficit exploded to $11.6 billion in the first seven months of the year against $6.5 billion a year earlier. The shortfall is mainly the result of plunging prices for semiconductors, steel and petrochemical products.

The consumer price index rose 5.3 percent in August on the year, up from a 3.5 percent rise a year earlier. For the first eight months of this year, the index gained 4.4 percent, just slightly off the year's 4.5 percent target.
Price stability has been the top priority of the South Korean government.
"The government believes managing inflation for the last quarter would be relatively easy because usually inflationary pressures during the period are not very heavy," said Shin.
However, some dealers said it was possible the central bank was not stepping in aggressively because it expects the won to rebound naturally.

"Corporate demand for won is generally strong prior to the Korean Thanksgiving Holiday," said Lee of LG, referring to the September 26 to 29 holiday. "Companies will have to sell dollars to prepare for bonus payments."
Moreover, an inflow of new funds when the foreign ownership ceiling in the stock market is raised in October is also likely to boost the won.
On October 1, the foreign limit will be eased to 20 percent from the current 18 percent.
